beliefs: f shifts the first character forward by one codepoint within its script: ASCII a-z/A-Z wrap within their case, accented Latin-1 letters shift codepoint+1 (é→ê, ñ→ò, ß→à, ü→ý, ÿ→Ā), Greek α→β, ω→ϖ, Cyrillic а→б, я→ѐ [E1, E3, E7, E8, E9]
f leaves the middle characters (positions 1..n-1) unchanged [E1, E2, E3, E4]
f appends a literal 'y' to the end of the string, but only if the string does not already end in 'y' [E5, E6]
Single-character input 'y' returns 'z' (shifted, no append since it already ends in y) [E4, E5]
When the first character is a digit, it is NOT shifted: '0a'->'0ay', '9z'->'9zy', '123'->'123y' [E1, E3]
The trailing 'y' is appended for non-empty inputs not ending in 'y', including digit-first ones ('0a'->'0ay', '9'->'9y') [E1, E2, E3]
The append is suppressed when the input already ends in 'y': 'ay'->'by', 'yyy'->'zyy', 'Yy'->'Zy' [E5]
Non-letter first characters (digits, space, punctuation) are left unchanged but still get the trailing 'y' if not already ending in 'y' [E6]
The shift is codepoint+1 for any letter, with case-preserving wrap only for ASCII a-z/A-Z; other scripts shift by codepoint+1 without wrapping (ω→ϖ, я→ѐ) [E8, E9]
The micro sign µ (U+00B5) IS shifted to ¶ (U+00B6), so it is treated as a letter despite being category Ll; other symbols like ¶, °, ±, ª are left unchanged [E15]
Whether non-ASCII letters wrap at their script's end (e.g. ω→α, я→а) is unclear; I use codepoint+1 with no wrap for non-ASCII [E9]?
